name: Bijim
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand sources agree (2 agree, 0 refine), none contradicts
catalog_citation: Norton, Russell J. 2019. Bijim Linguistics Consultant Report (research 10-13 October 2018, TCNN Bukuru; report dated 27 February 2019). Bukuru: SIL Nigeria, 15 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives item 84252.
catalog_locator: sec. 6 'Tones', p. 6 (txt); sec. 10 'Tone stability and downstep', p. 14 (txt); saved file
catalog_quote: Five tone classes L M H LH ML were confirmed by classifying CV, CVC, CCVC, CVCV and CVCVC words according to their tone, as shown in full below. Words sometimes varied between the LH class and the M class or (for one speaker) between the LH class and the L class. Participants chose to represent tone contrasts in writing by a doubled vowel for H tone or ‘h’ after the vowel for L tone, with M tone left unmarked. [p. 6] ... With these effects, the system reduces to an underlying two-tone L-H system with four underlying melodies /L/, /H/, /LH/ or /LHL/, of which the latter two instantiate downstep after a floating L, producing [ꜜH] and [ꜜHL] respectively. It is then doubtful whether the LH class and the M class are in a stable contrast, as the /LH/ melody is the basis for both and the difference lies only in whether the L tone is linked or not. [p. 14]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bijim is a tone language: lexical items fall into five surface tone classes (L, M, H, LH rising, ML falling) which Norton analyses as an underlying two-tone /L, H/ system with floating-L downstep. The source says nothing about word stress or accent; no accessible source states where stress falls or whether stress exists.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone classes LH and M (and for one speaker LH and L) vary; tone on syllabic nasals not assessed (p.13).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone on citation-form words elicited from a Blench 600-item wordlist in a participatory workshop with five speakers (Gambar, Aruti, Dukli, Yang villages); no phrase-level prosody, no stress discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Norton 2019 and the dictionary describe the Bijim variety [bij-17997] with speakers from Gambar, Aruti and Yang (Tafawa Balewa LGA, Bauchi State) and Dukli (Gindiri area, Plateau State); after ISO change request 2020-035 these lects are Bijim [jbm] = biji1246 (Decker et al. 2021 language code: Kaduk = Luggere, Gambar, Dukli Bauchi = Bijim [jbm]). The sister lects Kadung/Kwanka/Kwaŋ [dkg] and Tiyaa/Ya/Boi [tyy] are separate languages (Glottolog vagh1250 sisters); Blench 2007 (downloaded) describes Kadung, not Bijim. Glottolog still lists Blench 2022 under the name 'Vaghat' = Bijim.

new_statements.quote: Vaghat has three level tones as well as rising and falling tones, as shown in Table 13. [Table 13. Vaghat phonetic tones: H á High; M ā Mid; L à Low; HL â Falling; LM Low Rising; MH a᷄ Mid Rising] The rising tones are all of extremely low incidence, and it may be more economical to analyse them as sequences of two like vowels, as with numerals (see previous section). High tone is markedly less common than Mid and Low. The High-Low falling tone is restricted to verb roots.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement (Norton 2019: tone language, no stress statement). Tone inventory differs in detail: Blench gives three phonetic levels H M L plus contours, Norton gives five surface classes L M H LH ML reduced to underlying /L H/ with downstep; neither says anything about stress. The the Internet Archive academia.edu capture embeds the full paper text (title page through p. 16); two re-download attempts today failed by automated download rc=7 (no connection to web.archive.org), so the copy read is the file saved earlier today from the same URL.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Vaghat (= Bijim) is described as a tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) plus a falling HL tone (verb roots only) and rare rising tones; the paper's phonology section has no subsection on stress or accent and the words 'stress', 'accent' and 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the text. Nominal prefix tone is low by default but can be raised to mid by mid-tone stems (p. 11); the appendix (p. 16) calls tone 'the most problematic aspect of Vaghat' for orthography.
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress; tonal notes: rising tones extremely rare, HL falling restricted to verb roots, High tone less common than Mid and Low
new_statements.identity_note: Blench 2022 uses the name Vaghat [bij] and states in its abstract that 'Vaghat is the same as the Bijim and Legeri languages, listed in older sources'; it distinguishes Upland (U) and Lowland (L) dialects, differing in a tone-raising rule (Table 5, p. 6). ISO 639-3 CR 2020-035 split [bij] into Bijim [jbm], Kadung [dkg] and Tiyaa [tyy]; Blench 2018's 'Kwang' data are from the Kadung/Kwanka sister lect, not Bijim proper.
